The 40-mark total and the 24 content-and-organisation / 16 technical-accuracy split are printed on AQA's specimen question papers for 8700/1 and 8700/2; the AO5 and AO6 descriptions come from AQA's scheme of assessment. hero.text: Forty marks - a quarter of the whole qualification - for one piece of writing in about forty-five minutes. It is the most improvable question on either paper, and the one most often left the least time.

blocks.title: Original RCF practice material
text: Every prompt, example and model answer on this page was written by RCF English. They are not AQA questions and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced. AQA's own materials are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/aqa/papers/).

blocks.text: **Paper 1 Question 5 is worth 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).** You choose between writing a description suggested by a picture and writing the opening part of a story. AQA advises about 45 minutes for Section B.

blocks.heading: What the 40 marks are for
blocks.caption: The split is printed on the specimen question paper; the objective wording is summarised from AQA's scheme of assessment.
rows: Communicating clearly and imaginatively; choosing tone, style and register to suit form, purpose and audience; organising the whole piece so it holds together
A range of vocabulary and sentence structures used for effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation

blocks.title: Sixteen marks for accuracy is a fifth of the paper
text: AQA states that AO6 must account for 20% of the marks for the whole qualification. On this question it is 16 of the 40. That is more than Paper 1 Question 2 and Question 3 combined. Five minutes of checking at the end is the best-paid five minutes on the paper.

items.title: Choose in 60 seconds (RCF recommendation)
text: Description or narrative. Choose the one you have practised, not the one that looks easier. If you cannot picture an ending, do not choose the story.

items.title: Plan for 5 minutes
text: For a description: five things you will describe, in a deliberate order. For a narrative: the situation, the change, and the last line. Knowing the last line before you start is what keeps a story from wandering.

items.title: Write for 35 minutes
text: Aim for four to six paragraphs and roughly one and a half to two sides. Vary paragraph length deliberately: a one-sentence paragraph after three long ones lands hard.

items.title: Check for 5 minutes
text: Not for better words - for accuracy. Sentence boundaries, verb tenses, apostrophes, spelling of the words you used most. This is the AO6 sweep.

blocks.heading: Description: the structure that stops it drifting
text: A description has no plot, so it needs a shape imposed on it or it becomes a list of adjectives. The most reliable shape is a camera movement: start wide, narrow to one detail, then pull back out.

parts.heading: A five-part frame
numbered: **Wide.** The whole scene in two or three sentences.
**Closer.** One area of it, with sound and temperature as well as sight.
**One detail.** A single small object or movement, described at length. This is where the best writing usually happens.
**A person, or the absence of one.** Even a description benefits from something that can change.
**Back out.** Return to the wide view, altered by what we have just looked at closely.

parts.heading: Worked example: the closing two paragraphs of a description (original RCF)
text: On the third step from the bottom someone had left a single glove, palm upwards, fingers slightly curled, as though it had been dropped mid-gesture. It had been there long enough for the dust to settle into the creases and turn them grey. Nobody had moved it. Nobody, in a building of four hundred people, had thought it was theirs to move.

From the top of the stairwell the whole hall was visible again - the folded chairs, the long windows, the light going yellow along the far wall - and it looked exactly as it had ten minutes earlier, except that now it looked like a place where things got left.

blocks.heading: Narrative: opening part, not whole story
text: AQA's specimen paper asks for *the opening part* of a story. That instruction is a gift, and students routinely ignore it by cramming in a twist ending. You are not being asked to finish anything.
bullets: **Start in the middle of something.** A character already doing, already deciding, already too late.
**One change.** An opening needs a single thing to become different, not a plot.
**Withhold.** Tell the reader less than you know. A withheld fact is the cheapest tension available.

**End on a line that opens.** Not a resolution - a direction. Compare the ending of the extract on the [Paper 1 questions page](global-english/gcse/aqa/paper-1/questions/), where a character decides one thing and does another.
**Two characters at most.** Forty-five minutes cannot hold more.

blocks.heading: Original RCF model answer: the opening of a story

items.label: Task and model
items.prompt: Write the opening part of a story about a place that has been left empty. (Original RCF practice task, in the style of Paper 1 Question 5.)
sample: The keys still worked. That was the first thing, and Dara stood in the doorway for a moment holding them and feeling faintly cheated, as though a house left standing for six years ought to have had the decency to change its locks.

Inside, the hall smelled of nothing at all. She had expected damp, or the sweetish smell of a place that has been shut; instead there was an absence, thin and clean, like the inside of a jar. Her footsteps were louder than they should have been. She put them down more carefully after that, which she recognised as ridiculous even while she was doing it.

The kitchen was the room she had promised herself she would not go into first, so she went into it first. The table was where it had been. Someone - and there had only ever been one someone - had left a cup upside down on the draining board, and the ring of dust around its rim showed that it had been washed, dried and set down deliberately, by a person who intended to come back for it.
Dara looked at the cup for a long time.

Then she went out to the car for the boxes, and left the front door standing open behind her, because she had decided on the drive up that she would not be the kind of person who crept about in her own house, and it seemed important to start as she meant to go on.
notes: **Organisation (AO5).** Five paragraphs, each shorter or longer than the last on purpose. The four-word paragraph - *Dara looked at the cup for a long time* - carries the emotional weight precisely because everything around it is longer.
**Content (AO5).** One change only: a woman enters a house. No twist, no plot. The interest is entirely in what she notices and what she refuses to notice.
**Withholding.** We are never told who left, or why. "There had only ever been one someone" is the whole of the backstory, and it works because it is a fragment.

**Range (AO6).** Sentence forms vary from a three-word opening to a fifty-word closing sentence. The simile - *like the inside of a jar* - is unusual but concrete, which is what earns range marks rather than reaching for a longer word.
**The last line opens rather than closes**, which is exactly what *the opening part of a story* asks for.

blocks.heading: Question 5 checklist
items: Did I plan for five minutes before writing?
Does my piece have a deliberate shape - a beginning, a shift and an ending I chose in advance?
Have I varied paragraph length, including at least one very short one?
Have I varied sentence openings, so that not every sentence starts with the subject?
Have I used punctuation beyond the full stop - a colon, a semicolon, a dash - correctly?
Did I spend the last five minutes checking accuracy rather than adding words?
For a narrative: is this an **opening**, not a complete story with a twist?

blocks.heading: Creative writing at GCSE
do: Describe one thing at length rather than five things briefly.
Use concrete nouns. *A glove* is worth more than *various items*.
Let one short sentence do the emotional work.
Reread the last five words of each paragraph - they carry more weight than the first five.
Write about somewhere you can actually picture.
dont: Do not end with *and then I woke up*, or with a twist that cancels the piece.
Do not open with an alarm clock, and do not describe a character looking in a mirror.
Do not use a long word you are unsure how to spell - AO6 is 16 marks.
Do not write dialogue for its own sake; it eats time and rarely earns range marks.
Do not describe the picture prompt literally, item by item. It is *suggested by* the picture.

items.q: How long should my GCSE creative writing answer be?
a: There is no set length. In the 45 minutes AQA advises for Section B, most students who plan for five minutes and check for five produce between one and a half and two sides. Quality of organisation and accuracy are marked; word count is not.

Neither is marked more generously - both are assessed on the same 24 and 16 marks. Description suits students who can hold a shape without a plot; narrative suits students who can resist finishing the story. Choose the one you have practised.

items.q: Do I have to describe the picture exactly?
a: No. The task is to write a description *suggested by* the picture, so the image is a starting point rather than a subject to inventory. A piece that begins in the picture and moves somewhere of its own is entirely acceptable.

items.q: How much do spelling and punctuation actually matter?
a: A great deal: 16 of the 40 marks are for technical accuracy, and AQA requires this objective to be 20% of the marks for the whole qualification. A well-shaped piece with weak accuracy loses more than students expect.

pages.title: AQA Paper 2 Transactional Writing

pages.description: AQA English Language Paper 2 Question 5 explained: writing to present a point of view in articles, letters, speeches and essays, with a model answer and practice.
pages.keywords: AQA paper 2 question 5, transactional writing GCSE, GCSE writing to argue, AQA viewpoint writing, GCSE article writing model answer

hero.text: Forty marks for one piece of writing that argues a case. The form is named for you, the audience is named for you, and both are marked.

blocks.title: Original RCF practice material
text: Every prompt, example and model answer here was written by RCF English. They are not AQA questions and no AQA mark scheme wording is reproduced.

blocks.text: **Paper 2 Question 5 is worth 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).** You are given a statement and asked to write presenting your point of view, in a stated form - an article, a letter, a speech, an essay or a leaflet - for a stated audience. AQA advises about 45 minutes for Section B.

blocks.heading: The forms, and what gives each one away
blocks.caption: Form is part of the content and organisation mark. An examiner should be able to name the form from the first three lines.
rows: A headline, then a hook - a question, a scene, a surprising fact
Dear Sir or Madam / Dear Mrs Bhatt, then your reason for writing
Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely, and a request
Address the audience: Good morning, everyone
Spoken rhythm, direct address, rhetorical questions
The issue stated without repeating the question
Your view, stated once, at the end
Leaflet or text for a website
What the reader should do next

items.title: Decide your line in 2 minutes
text: Agree, disagree, or agree with a limit. Any of the three earns full marks; changing your mind in paragraph four does not. Write your position at the top of the page and keep looking at it.

items.title: Plan three arguments in 3 minutes (RCF recommendation)
text: Three reasons, each with one example. Order them weakest to strongest, so the piece gains force. Add one counter-argument you will concede and answer.

items.title: Write for 35 minutes
text: Introduction, three argument paragraphs, one counter-argument paragraph, conclusion. Six paragraphs is a comfortable shape for the time.

items.title: Check for 5 minutes
text: Accuracy only. Sixteen marks are waiting here.

blocks.heading: The counter-argument paragraph is worth writing
text: A piece that only asserts sounds like a pupil. A piece that concedes something and then answers it sounds like a writer. It costs one paragraph and it lifts the content and organisation mark more reliably than any rhetorical device.
bullets: **Limit the concession:** *What this argument overlooks is...*
**Return to your line:** *Which is precisely why...*

blocks.heading: Original RCF model answer: an article

items.label: Task and model (opening, one argument, the counter-argument, ending)
items.prompt: "Students should be required to do at least one hour of unpaid work for their community each week. It would teach them more than any lesson." Write an article for a newspaper in which you explain your point of view on this statement. (Original RCF practice task, in the style of Paper 2 Question 5.)
sample: Last winter my neighbour spent every Saturday morning driving elderly people to a supermarket eleven miles away. Nobody made him do it. That, I have come to think, is the entire reason it worked - and the entire reason this proposal will not.

The argument for compulsory community work is not stupid, and it is worth stating fairly. Young people who have volunteered do report that it changed how they see their town. They meet people whose lives are nothing like theirs. They discover that a bus timetable is a political document. None of this is taught anywhere on a school timetable, and none of it is easily taught at all.

But the word doing the damage in this proposal is *required*. An hour that has been demanded is not a gift, and everyone involved knows it - including, most painfully, the person receiving it. There is a particular indignity in being helped by someone who is being marked for helping you, and I have never seen that indignity acknowledged by anyone advocating this scheme.

It is perfectly true that we require plenty of things whose value teenagers cannot yet see; nobody waits for a fourteen-year-old to develop a spontaneous enthusiasm for algebra. What that argument overlooks is that algebra does not have feelings. Compulsory kindness has a second party, and that party can tell.

There is a better version of this idea, and it is unglamorous: make volunteering easy rather than compulsory. Publish what needs doing. Arrange the transport. Let students go once and come back if they want to. My neighbour did not need a policy. He needed a car and a list.
Requiring people to be good is the shortest route to producing people who resent being good. If we want a generation that turns up, we should stop marking the register.
notes: **Form is unmistakable.** A headline, an anecdotal hook, direct address to a general readership, and a closing line that turns rather than summarises. An examiner names the form in three seconds.

**Content and organisation (AO5).** One line of argument held from the first paragraph to the last. The structure moves weakest to strongest: concede the case, isolate the flaw, answer the obvious objection, propose an alternative, close.
**The counter-argument paragraph does real work.** It concedes something genuine, then limits the concession with a distinction - *algebra does not have feelings* - rather than dismissing it.

**Technical accuracy and range (AO6).** Sentence lengths vary sharply; the shortest sentence in the piece, *That party can tell*, is placed where the argument turns. The italicised single word *required* isolates the point without needing a paragraph of explanation.
**The return at the end.** The neighbour from paragraph one comes back in paragraph six, which closes the loop and makes the argument feel finished rather than stopped.

blocks.heading: Practice, then check your own
text: **Original RCF practice task.** "Every school should abolish homework for students under fourteen and replace it with reading." Write a speech for your school's governing body in which you explain your point of view. 45 minutes. Then work through this list.
items: Can a reader name the form from my first three lines?
Have I addressed the audience the task named, not a general reader?
Is my position identical in paragraph one and paragraph six?
Do I have three arguments, each with an example rather than an assertion?
Have I conceded one thing and answered it?
Have I varied sentence length deliberately, including at least one very short sentence at a turning point?
Did I spend five minutes on accuracy at the end?

items.q: Do I have to agree with the statement?
a: No. You are asked to explain your point of view, and disagreement, agreement and a qualified position are all worth full marks. What is marked is how clearly and effectively you communicate the view you take, not the view itself.

items.q: How many rhetorical devices should I use?
a: As many as the argument needs and no more. A list of three, a rhetorical question and a piece of direct address are useful when they carry a point; strung together for their own sake they read as a technique checklist and do not lift the content and organisation mark. One well-placed short sentence usually does more than three rhetorical questions.

No. Invented figures are transparent and they weaken a piece. Specific, plausible detail from your own experience is more persuasive and costs nothing - the neighbour with the car in the model answer above does more work than any percentage would.

items.q: Does the form really matter if the writing is good?
a: Yes. AO5 covers selecting and adapting tone, style and register for different forms, purposes and audiences, so a strong essay submitted where a speech was asked for has left part of the objective unmet.
